look_here_first: GIANT CUTGRASS: look for a TALL coarse rhizomatous emergent marsh grass, broad saw-edged blades and an unusually large open to drooping many-branched panicle. Its separate MALE and FEMALE one-flowered spikelets occur on the SAME panicle branches; modern Kew and USGS/NOAA treatments place MALE spikelets BASAL and FEMALE spikelets toward branch tips, but older botanical descriptions REVERSE the positions. Confirm male anthers versus female stigma/fruit before applying any position-based rule; do not identify sex from head silhouette. Find the true LONG papery MEMBRANOUS ligule at a fresh blade–sheath junction, Kew usually 6–20 mm — not a tiny hair fringe. Confirm actual sex characters/spikelets with hand lens and mm scale. One Florida source photograph documents flowering-head form, not a Hays locality voucher.

best_field_traits: Very robust rhizomatous perennial rooted in fresh or mildly brackish marshes, ponds and stream banks; source-based, no new county occurrence claim.
Reedlike 2–3 m flowering culms with long, broad, sharply serrulate-edged blades (Kew 50–150 cm × 8–22 mm).
Large generally open, often drooping panicle about 30–60 cm; multiple branches rather than a fluffy Phragmites plume.

Separate one-flowered male and female spikelets occur on the SAME panicle branches. Kew and modern USGS/NOAA accounts place MALE toward the base and FEMALE toward the tip, but historical treatments reverse the arrangement; verify sex by anthers or stigma/fruit, not position alone.
Distinctive LONG eciliate membranous ligule at fresh blade/sheath junction ~6–20 mm; not short ciliate ligule characteristic of some other wetland grasses.
Female fertile spikelets usually 6–8 mm, short-awned fertile lemma (~2–3-mm awn), and absent/obscure basal glumes (Kew). Needs a true dissected macro.
Leaf-margin teeth are sharp; do not slide bare fingers along blade or pull protected aquatic vegetation.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: WHOLE rooted marsh stand with flowering culm and broad attached leaf from same plant; no unnecessary rhizome excavation.
10–20× backlit leaf-margin serrulations with true arrow direction and 1-mm ruler, no barehand rubbing.
TRUE long membranous ligule unfolded at blade–sheath junction with ruler (Kew 6–20 mm); clearly contrast hair-fringe of comparison grasses.

SAME panicle branch displaying lower MALE (staminate/anther-bearing) and upper FEMALE (pistillate/stigma or fruit) spikelets, each actually photographed and source-ID confirmed before individual arrows.
One mature 6–8 mm female spikelet with 2–3 mm lemma awn, true glume base, separate anthers and stigma photographed under ruler.
Side-by-side verified native lineage Phragmites, invasive Arundo donax, smaller Leersia oryzoides, and endangered Zizania texana without collecting rare river plants.
crew_field_check: FIRST: giant tall wetland grass in often pure stand, but this is only a habitat/growth-form clue.
SECOND: seek a very large, arching loose-branched head; do not mistake it for the dense feathery plume of Phragmites or the bulky Arundo plume.
THIRD: unfold fresh blade/sheath junction: Zizaniopsis has a remarkably LONG paperlike ligule, ~6–20 mm (Kew). Measure instead of imagining it from whole-plant photographs.

FOURTH: examine several spikelets on ONE branch under lens, checking actual anthers against stigmas/fruit. Contemporary Kew/USGS places MALE basal and FEMALE terminal, but older descriptions disagree; do not arrow sexes from position or unverified existing overview photographs.
FIFTH: compare real tiny rough-margin teeth in a leaf micrograph, then verify one-flowered, glume-reduced female spikelet and short terminal awn (not shown here).
SIXTH: prioritize no-disturbance identification around the protected San Marcos River Texas wild-rice; do not dig in, handle or collect Zizania texana.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Giant cutgrass Zizaniopsis has tall coarse marsh growth; BROAD sharp-serrulate blades; a great loose 30–60-cm panicle with distinct separate one-flowered MALE and FEMALE spikelets on each branch (male basal/female terminal in modern treatments; historical accounts conflict, so verify actual sexual organs); and an unusually LONG membranous 6–20-mm ligule. Phragmites australis can have a distinctly feathery soft panicle; includes Texas native and introduced lineages, so a single morphology photograph does not certify invasion status. Introduced Arundo donax has a robust fluffy plume, bamboo-like cane and different spikelet/ligule details. Leersia oryzoides is generally smaller and has much smaller flattened narrow rice-shaped spikelets and tiny backward-pointing leaf teeth. Protected Zizania texana is aquatic wild-rice endemic to the San Marcos River and must not be handled for photographs. Tripsacum's thick single flowering spikes carry male units ABOVE female bead-like joints, opposite the mixed sex positions along Zizaniopsis panicle branches. Use paired reproductive/ligule photos before final call.

measured_reproductive_key_20261023.look_here_first: On a coarse rhizomatous wetland grass, find the long 6–20 mm membranous ligule. Follow one open panicle branch and identify MALE by anthers and FEMALE by stigma/fruit. Modern Kew/USGS place males basal and females terminal; older sources reverse this, so do not use branch position alone.
measured_diagnostic_key: GROWTH: large rhizomatous perennial with broad sharp-serrulate leaves; flowering culms often 2–3 m. Never infer Hays County provenance from an out-of-state photo.
PANICLE: Kew 30–60 cm, open, with separate male and female one-flowered spikelets on the same branches; male below female.
FEMALE spikelet: Kew 6–8 mm, one fertile floret, ovate/laterally compressed; two glumes absent or obscure. Female lemma 6–8 mm, 7-veined, single terminal awn 2–3 mm; palea ~lemma length, 3-veined.
MALE spikelet: Kew 6–8 mm, one floret, glumes absent, 7-veined lemma AWNLESS (muticous); six anthers. Male and female units cannot be differentiated confidently from a distant head photograph.
LIGULE: long eciliate membranous flap 6–20 mm at fresh inner blade/sheath junction; measure, do not label the exterior collar.

AWN/GLUME WARNING: male lemma is awnless while female lemma is short-awned; neither sex has ordinary conspicuous paired glumes. Do not mistake lemma for glume or label an awn from a whole-panicle photo.
measured_reproductive_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: Phragmites australis: dense feathery plume and distinct multiflowered spikelet anatomy; native versus introduced lineage unresolved by silhouette. Arundo donax: cane-like clumps, conspicuous hairy lemma florets, not sex-separated panicle spikelets. Tripsacum dactyloides: male units ABOVE female on a thick jointed flowering spike, not below on an open panicle branch. Leersia oryzoides: smaller narrow rice-like spikelets and different growth form. Do not disturb protected Zizania texana.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Giant cutgrass — 8 archived real photos, long ligule and sex-verified spikelets still needed
steps: START with EIGHT archived exact-source giant cutgrass JPEGs: Florida flowering head and wetland habit, Texas joined basal shoots, Dallas attached panicle branches and actual orange ANTHERS. None establishes a Hays County voucher; the Anahuac crown does not expose underground rhizomes.

At actual exterior sheath panel 2, locate where the blade enters the sheath, but do NOT label this as the opened 6–20-mm TRUE papery ligule. A separate inside-collar view with 1-mm ruler is still missing.

Use panel 7 for genuine orange extruded ANTHERS (male organ); panels 4 and 6 for close floral architecture, not certified female spikelets. Kew/USGS/NOAA and older North American treatments disagree on sex POSITION; document anther versus stigma/fruit on the SAME vouchered branch before any positional arrow.

Published spikelets of both sexes ~6–8 mm; female fertile lemma seven-veined with ~2–3-mm awn, male lemma awnless, glumes absent/obscure. Actual calibrated separate male/female spikelet and lemma dissections remain missing; do not reuse a general flower macro as that proof.

The real Texas Anahuac basal crown panel 5 is ALREADY available; next high-value vegetative images are underground rhizome connection and 10–20× serrulate blade margin with mm scale. Avoid destructive collection and handling sharp margins barehanded.

Different-species comparison panels 8–10 are Arundo, Phragmites (lineage UNKNOWN) and protected Zizania texana. Use verified individual florets and panicle architecture; do not infer nativity, invasive status or reed lineage from wet habitat.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: 6–20 mm true membranous ligule + saw-edged wide blades + very large open wetland panicle + documented unisexual spikelets; genital position needs voucher-paired photos due historical-treatment discrepancy.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Eight source-labelled species JPEGs are physically archived: original CC BY 4.0 photographs plus individually CC BY-NC 4.0 Texas basal/branch images. Existing 11 panels include 3 clearly different-species comparisons. Male anthers are actually visible, but the female spikelet, opened 6–20-mm ligule, 2–3-mm female awn insertion, leaf teeth and underground rhizome remain unverified. Modern/historical sex-position conflict is a SCIENTIFIC HOLD. No new photos/arrows or Pages verification in this finalization.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · GIANT MARSH GRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Broad sharp-edged leaves and a large open wetland panicle
field_id_short_tiles.details: Find a tall coarse emergent marsh grass with broad serrulate blades and open 30–60 cm flowering panicle. Existing Florida head and habitat panels (0,1) plus real whole wetland growth (3) show habit. Texas Anahuac panel 5 shows ACTUAL joined basal shoots and fibrous rootlike material, but NOT an exposed underground rhizome or a Hays voucher. Culms ~2–3 m and rhizomatous habit are published descriptions, not measurements from these images.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE LONG LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Open the collar: look for a 6–20 mm papery membrane
field_id_short_tiles.details: The true eciliate membrane is on the inner blade/sheath junction, not the external node shown in panel 3. Published Kew measurement 6–20 mm. No current image proves the opened ligule with a ruler.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MALE AND FEMALE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Both sexes occur on the same branch—identify the organs first
field_id_short_tiles.details: TRUE new organ evidence: gallery panel 7 (zero-based) shows orange EXSERTED ANTHERS on a source-identified Dallas flowering branch; panel 6 shows attached Texas branchlet spikelets, but does not resolve each spikelet's sex. Panel 4 has pale feathery floral parts whose exact stigma identity is not certified. Male anthers and female stigmas/fruits must be documented together on ONE vouchered branch at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler before mapping sex position. Modern Kew/USGS/NOAA place male toward branch bases and female toward tips; an older description reverses it. Do NOT arrow unverified female organs or infer sex from branch location. Published individual spikelets ~6–8 mm; glumes absent or obscure in modern Kew.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL ANTHERS PHOTOGRAPHED — FEMALE SPIKELET/SEX POSITION UNVERIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA, AWN AND LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Female short-awned lemma; male lemma awnless
field_id_short_tiles.details: Kew reports female lemma 6–8 mm, seven-veined, with one 2–3 mm awn; male lemma awnless. Require actual 10–20× dissections with scale, then distinguish Phragmites's many-flowered silky plume, Arundo's plume, Tripsacum's jointed spike, and Leersia's smaller rice-like spikelets. Do not disturb endangered Zizania texana.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · LEAF TEETH AND BASE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Find sharp blade edges on a connected rhizomatous culm
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow broad ~8–22-mm blades down to a tall reedlike culm. Existing panel 2 documents a real exterior sheath/node, NOT the opened long inner ligule. New Anahuac Texas panel 5 demonstrates joined basal shoots, old sheaths and rootlike fibers, NOT a photographed underground connecting rhizome. Leaf edges are reported serrulate; a 10–20× 1-mm-scaled image of actual margin teeth is still missing. Avoid sliding bare fingers along the blade or destructively collecting sensitive marsh plants.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL BASAL CROWN PHOTO — RHIZOME/MARGIN TEETH STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · REED OR CUTGRASS?
field_id_short_tiles.short: Check real florets before calling a tall marsh grass
field_id_short_tiles.details: Use real giant-cutgrass open panicle (panel 0) and clearly DIFFERENT-SPECIES look-alike panels: Arundo donax (8), Phragmites australis of unresolved lineage (9), and protected Texas wild-rice Zizania texana (10). Phragmites/Arundo have silky multi-flowered plume spikelets; Zizaniopsis has separate one-flowered male and female spikelets, with real male anthers in target panel 7 but no same-branch confirmed female organs yet. Tripsacum dactyloides has jointed spikes with male units above female hard joints; Leersia oryzoides is smaller. Published Zizaniopsis female lemma ~6–8 mm with ~2–3 mm awn; male lemma awnless. Do not arrow unverified reproductive sex, label Phragmites lineage from habit, or disturb endangered Zizania texana.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE PANELS INSTALLED — SEX-CONFIRMED SPIKELET DISSECTION MISSING

grass_species_finalization_20261025.look_here_first: Broad sharp-edged rhizomatous marsh grass with open 30–60 cm panicle; measure true inner 6–20 mm ligule, then distinguish one-flowered male/anther-bearing and female/stigma-bearing spikelets on same branch without assuming position.

All source-based, NOT measurements from present images.

Arundo donax (silky multi-flowered lemma plume, giant cane)
Tripsacum dactyloides (thick spike with male upper/female jointed lower)
Zizania texana (protected endemic, do not collect or disturb)

grass_species_finalization_20261025.scientific_holds: Modern Kew/USGS/NOAA descriptions put male spikelets basally and female terminally; historical Hitchcock/Lamson-Scribner reverses this. Treat sex-position as unresolved for photographic arrows until organ-level same-branch voucher. Preserve existing county-native and taxonomy holds.
